texto:
Google on October 30, 2026 set out the scale of DevFest 2026, its annual series of developer conferences run by local volunteer groups: more than 800 events in 115 countries between October 1 and December 31, with almost 1 million attendees expected to learn how to "build, secure, and scale in the agentic era." The post appeared a month after the series had begun. One of those events, Lisbon DevFest 2026 on Saturday, November 28, shows what the brief looks like on the ground: 13 sessions in a single day, 11 of them built around AI tools, Gemini or AI agents.
In Short
Google helps volunteer groups run hundreds of one-day conferences for software developers around the world, and it says more than 800 of them will take place by the end of 2026. In Lisbon, almost every talk on November 28 is about building with AI, including AI agents that carry out tasks without step-by-step instructions. The tools taught at these events are the same ones now turning up in ad tech, analytics and publisher software, so the agenda gives an early view of what the people who build marketing systems are learning next.
800 events, 92 days
The announcement was published on the Google Developers Blog under the title "DevFest is back!", written by Natalie McHugh, a Developer Relations Program Manager at Google. It describes DevFest as "the world's largest, annual, community-led event series aimed to educate developers and builders about Google's latest technologies."
The figures are compact. Hosted by Google Developer Groups (GDG), DevFest runs from October 1 through December 31, 2026. "Across 800+ global events, almost 1 million attendees will gather across 115 countries," according to the post. Sessions and workshops focus on "the latest Google AI technologies," with additional tracks for Google Cloud, Android and Web, which Google says give developers "actionable tools to deploy real-world solutions."
The wording of the theme matters more than it might appear. "Agentic era" is the phrase Google uses for its shift towards agentic AI, software that plans and executes multi-step tasks rather than answering one prompt at a time. At Google I/O in May, a 41-minute panel published on the Google for Developers YouTube channel was titled "Defining the agentic AI era". DevFest carries the same message to local communities.
Some arithmetic puts the scale in proportion. The window spans 92 days, so 800 events works out at about 8.7 per day, and about seven per country on average, according to PPC Land's calculation. If both of Google's figures held, the average event would draw about 1,250 people. The post was published on day 30 of the window, when roughly a third of the period had already passed.
What the post does not provide is equally relevant. It gives no count of events already held, no breakdown by country or region, and no explanation of how "almost 1 million" was arrived at - whether the number reflects registrations to date, a forecast, or attendance in previous years. All of the figures are Google's own and none is independently audited. Google points readers to goo.gle/devfest to find in-person and virtual events, and asks attendees to post with the hashtag #DevFest.
Volunteer-run, Google-briefed
Google stresses the local character of the series. "DevFest is uniquely built by the community, for the community," according to the post. Events are "hosted in local languages by grassroots organizers," each "tailored to its regional ecosystem," with speakers drawn from Google Developer Experts (GDEs), Google engineers and local practitioners. "At its heart, DevFest is about community-driven problem-solving," the post says.
Two examples illustrate the claim. In Ireland, when two deaf attendees faced a shortage of interpreters, local GDG organisers built a real-time transcription tool with Google technologies within two weeks, according to Google. In Tashkent, more than 5,000 participants, ranging from university students to national digital leaders, gathered "to launch collaborative projects and accelerate regional tech growth." The post does not say in which year either event took place. The Tashkent figure is four times the average that Google's 2026 projections imply, by PPC Land's calculation, and an average of that kind says little about any single event.
The community framing sits alongside a content brief set by Google. By Google's own description, the series exists to teach Google's technologies. The Lisbon event page lists Google Portugal as its Diamond Venue Sponsor and Google for Developers as its Official Program Partner. Volunteers organise the day; Google sponsors the venue, supplies the subject matter and, through its expert programme, a large share of the speakers.
Lisbon on November 28
Lisbon DevFest 2026 takes place on Saturday, November 28, at AIhub by Unicorn Factory Lisboa, 38 Rua João Saraiva, in the Alvalade district, according to the GDG Lisbon event page. The page opens with a bilingual greeting - "Lisbon says Olá, temos festa to DevFest once again!" - and lists six key themes: AI, Android, DevFest, Google Cloud, Web, and workshops or hands-on sessions. On October 31, four weeks before the event, the page showed 45 RSVPs.
The page gives two different time windows. Its event listing says 10:30 AM to 7:00 PM, marked GMT+1. The official agenda further down starts with check-in at 08:30 and ends with "Closing & Raffles" at 18:00. The page does not reconcile the two. Mainland Portugal left summer time on October 25, so Lisbon will be on GMT on the day.
The event page lists five organisers from GDG Lisbon: Eimy Blanco, an Android developer at Appning by Forvia; Liliana Pereira, a software engineer at Coverflex; Nuno João Andrade, a senior developer; Priscila Peres Rodrigues of Ponts Network; and Cristiana Pereira, a marketing specialist. Thirteen speakers appear on the agenda. Five carry the GDE label, and one, Paulo Ramos, is a Customer Engineer at Google, so six of the 13 either work for Google or belong to its expert programme, according to PPC Land's count.
A day of agents
The programme runs on two tracks after the first coffee break, an auditorium and a workshop room hosting three 90-minute workshops. By PPC Land's count, 11 of the 13 sessions name AI, Gemini, agents, vibe coding or Google's Antigravity development environment in their titles. The two exceptions deal with Kubernetes resource planning and web performance.
The morning opens at 09:15 with Faith Njah, a technology advocate at Algo Coding Experts, on "The Weekend Founder: How Far Can Google's AI Stack Take You?" At 10:15, Ramos takes the auditorium for "Faces, Voices & Pixels: Building Real-Time AI Experiences That See, Speak and Create," while Jaime Blasco, a senior Flutter engineer at Sparkli and a GDE, runs the first workshop, "Chef Gemini: Building a Real-Time Kitchen Assistant with Live AI and Flutter." Liliana Romão of Grupo Nabeiro follows at 11:00 with a question rather than a promise: "AI for productivity - Is it?" A sponsor showcase closes the morning before lunch.
The afternoon is heavier on agents. Madalena Costa, an AI product experience strategist and host of Human x Intelligent, leads a 90-minute workshop called "Delegate or keep? Build a human-in-the-loop agent with Gemini", a title that frames the session around which tasks to hand to an agent and which to keep under human review. In the auditorium, Thalyta Sousa Mendonça, a cloud and DevOps engineer at Richemont, argues that "Kubernetes Resource Requests Are Not a Guessing Game." Hugo Alves, founder of Forge, speaks on "More Power to You: AI, Affordable Competence and David vs Goliath." Igor Rybakou, an engineering manager at Intapp, covers "How specialized AI agents assist throughout the software development lifecycle."
Security gets its own slot. Bianca Ximenes, a GDE in AI and machine learning, asks "The current status of AI agents: are sentient hacker systems coming to get us?" Later, Chiraz Chahbani, a GDE in Cloud, presents on vibe coding - building software by describing it in plain language and accepting what the model generates - in a talk titled "Vibe Coding: From Idea to Reality."
The final workshop is the one most directly connected to advertising technology. Dominika Zając, a senior software engineer and team lead at Qualtrics and a GDE, runs a debugging session built on Antigravity and Chrome DevTools MCP, the Model Context Protocol server that lets an AI coding agent inspect a live browser, under the title "Stop Guessing, Start Debugging." Medhat Dawoud, a senior software engineer at Miro and a GDE for Web, follows with "Build a Website that Works Great in the Worst User Conditions," and Nuno João Andrade closes the talks with "Crowdsourcing the Grid: Real-Time Power Simulation and AI Forecasting at Scale."
The agenda has a few loose ends. Mendonça's Kubernetes talk and Costa's 90-minute workshop are both listed under a 13:15 to 13:30 slot, a quarter of an hour after lunch ends. Costa's name is spelled "Madalena" in the agenda and "Madelena" in the speaker list. The page closes with an instruction to attendees: "Don't forget to bring your laptop for the interactive workshops and plenty of questions for our speakers."
Two versions of the theme
The Lisbon page frames 2026 differently from Google's post. It says this year's DevFest "will focus on empowering developer communities worldwide to 'architect the future of tech'," and describes the local goal as equipping developers "to build innovative, scalable, and ethically sound applications." It also says "last year's DevFest theme focused on building safe, secure, and scalable solutions" - wording that is close to the "build, secure, and scale" line Google uses as the global headline for 2026. Neither page explains the overlap.
A Gemini tag in the sponsor links
One detail on the Lisbon page is of particular interest to anyone who measures web traffic. The two sponsor links in the event description, pointing to Google Portugal's about page and to developers.google.com, both carry the tracking parameter "utm_source=gemini." Who gets the credit for a click on them? Any analytics tool that reads UTM parameters will attribute those visits to a source named gemini, even though the click comes from a GDG community page rather than from Google's AI assistant.
The page does not say how the description was written. AI assistants have begun attaching such tags to links in their answers: ChatGPT, for example, added utm_source=chatgpt to links in its "More" section in June 2025. When such a tag survives in text pasted onto an ordinary website, it travels with every click.
That matters because AI referral traffic has become a reporting category of its own. In May 2026, Google Analytics added a native AI Assistant channel to its default channel group, classifying traffic from ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and others when it detects a referrer that matches a recognised assistant. At launch, Google's Help Center did not specify which assistants were recognised. Links copied out of chatbot answers and republished elsewhere add a further source of noise: traffic labelled as coming from an assistant may have passed through a human-edited page first. On this page, the visits in question go to two Google properties, so any misattribution would show up in Google's own analytics.
Why the developer agenda reaches marketing
DevFest has no advertising track. The global post names no advertising or measurement products, and none of the 13 Lisbon sessions concerns the Google Ads API, Google Analytics or Ad Manager. Google runs a separate channel for that audience: in July 2025, its Ads Developer Relations team launched a Discord server for advertising developers, which had 14,854 members at launch.
Yet the tools on the Lisbon agenda are already part of advertising and publishing infrastructure. Chrome DevTools MCP, the subject of Zając's workshop, appeared in an AdSense email to publishers on March 24, 2026 that recommended AI-assisted debugging alongside bfcache and speculation rules. In August, Prebid.js merged a DevTools MCP module that lets AI agents read live header bidding auctions, events and TTL values through the same Chrome interface. Engineers who maintain Prebid wrappers, tag managers and measurement scripts already work with the tooling such workshops teach.
Antigravity has a short history. Google introduced it with Gemini 3 in November 2025 as an agent-first development environment, and at Google I/O on May 19, 2026 presented Antigravity 2.0 together with an Antigravity command-line tool, an SDK for self-hosted agents and Managed Agents in the Gemini API. The same keynote pushed WebMCP as a proposed web standard, and Chrome 149 opened a WebMCP origin trial that lets sites register tools that agents can call.
The volumes give a sense of what is at stake for Google in teaching these tools at community events. Alphabet reported on October 28, 2026 that its first-party model APIs were processing nearly 32 billion tokens per minute and that the Gemini app had passed 1 billion monthly users, up from 650 million a year earlier. Every developer who builds on Gemini after a DevFest workshop adds to that consumption.
The "secure" part of the theme has its own backdrop. Google redesigned AI Studio around vibe coding in October 2025, promising a path "from prompt to working AI app in minutes." In May 2026, research by the security firm RedAccess, reported by WIRED, found more than 5,000 public apps built on Lovable, Replit, Base44 and Netlify with essentially no authentication, close to 2,000 of which appeared to expose private corporate or personal data. Cost control belongs to "scale": on October 8, 2026, Google Cloud added project spend caps that pause a project's Gemini agent once a hard limit on AI spend is reached.
Lisbon has come up in Google's European event planning before. In June 2026, Google's Search Relations team listed Lisbon among six candidate cities for its first European Search Central Live Deep Dive, alongside Barcelona, Budapest, Berlin, Frankfurt and Prague.
What remains unclear
Several questions are left open by the two pages. Google does not say how many DevFest events had taken place by October 30, how attendance is counted, or whether virtual attendees are included in the almost 1 million figure. The Ireland and Tashkent examples carry no dates. Neither page gives a ticket price. In Lisbon, the start and finish times differ between the event listing and the agenda, and 45 RSVPs four weeks out says little about final attendance at a venue whose capacity the page does not state. What is clear is the emphasis: the global brief leads with Google's AI technologies and agents, with Cloud, Android and Web as supporting tracks.

Summary
Who: Google, through its Developer Relations team and Natalie McHugh, Developer Relations Program Manager; Google Developer Groups worldwide; GDG Lisbon and its five organisers; 13 Lisbon speakers, five of them Google Developer Experts and one a Google Customer Engineer.
What: Google announced the scale of DevFest 2026, a community-run developer conference series of more than 800 events in 115 countries expected to draw almost 1 million attendees, themed "build, secure, and scale in the agentic era." Lisbon's event lists 13 sessions, 11 of them on AI tools, Gemini or AI agents by PPC Land's count, and its sponsor links carry a utm_source=gemini tracking tag.
When: The announcement was published on October 30, 2026. The series runs from October 1 to December 31, 2026. Lisbon DevFest 2026 takes place on Saturday, November 28, 2026.
Where: Events take place in person and online in 115 countries. The Lisbon event is at AIhub by Unicorn Factory Lisboa, 38 Rua João Saraiva, in Lisbon's Alvalade district.
Why: Google uses DevFest to teach its AI, Cloud, Android and Web technologies to developers through local volunteer groups. For the marketing community, the agenda matters because the tools on it, including Chrome DevTools MCP, Antigravity and Gemini agents, are already entering ad tech code such as Prebid.js and publisher tooling such as AdSense recommendations, while AI-generated tracking tags complicate how AI referral traffic is measured.
